source_text:
COMFREY.

Descript :] The common Comfrey hath divers great and long green leaves lying upon the ground, so hairy or prickly, that if they touch any tender part of the hands, face, or body, it will cause it to itch. The flowers grow at the tops of the stalks, of a pale whitish colour, after which come small black seeds. The roots are great and long, black on the outside, and white or yellowish within, containing a clammy juice.

Names :] It is called of the Latins Consolida, of the English Comfrey, Consound, and Knit-back; the root whereof is chief in use.

Government and virtues :] It is under the dominion of Saturn, and surely no man of sound judgement will put it under Jupiter. The roots, while they are fresh and moist, being stamped small and boiled in water or wine until they are tender, and given to drink, do ease inward hurts, and inward ulcers, and knit the sinews that have been slack, and are of notable efficacy against spitting of blood. A plaster made hereof with mutton tallow, doth solder and glue together bleeding wounds, and is a special remedy for the bloody flux. Galen saith, it is cold and dry, of a healing and glewing nature. Dioscorides holds, that the root, boiled and given to drink, doth help spitting of blood, and them that make bloody water. Some hold, that it is good for the gout; but therein it faileth. The distilled water hereof is given for those purposes; yet the root is more effectual, and chiefly a decoction of it.

resolutions.reasoning: Culpeper's 'Comfrey / Consolida' with large hairy leaves and black clamy roots matches Symphytum officinale, the common comfrey of 17th-century English herbals; POWO returns an exact accepted-name match and the morphological description is consistent.

candidates.matched_via: regional vernacular 'consound' recorded for tuberous comfrey

resolutions.reasoning: 'Consound' is documented for both common and tuberous comfrey in early-modern glossaries. The entry context (single herb, clamy root) favours S. officinale, but the vernacular alone does not exclude S. tuberosum; kept ambiguous with a soft selection.

No lexical or authority source returns 'Knit-back'. It is plausibly a regional common name for S. officinale ('knitbone'), but no historical glossary available to the resolver confirms it; left unresolved rather than guessing.

ema_monograph.title: Symphyti radix (comfrey root) — EMA/HMPC community monograph
ema_monograph.relevance_note: Traditional use only, for bruises and sprains; restricted to unbroken skin, limited duration and age range — internal use is not accepted.

pubmed.title: Hepatotoxicity due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid-containing herbs: an update
pubmed.relevance_note: Documents hepatotoxicity of comfrey PAs; directly bears on Culpeper's internal decoction.

pubmed.title: Topical comfrey (Symphytum officinale) root extract in the treatment of ankle sprains: a randomised controlled trial
pubmed.relevance_note: Supports topical wound/trauma direction with clinical evidence.

pubmed.title: Allantoin and rosmarinic acid in Symphytum officinale root: wound-repair mechanisms in vitro
pubmed.relevance_note: Plausible mechanism for the historical 'knitting' claims.

evidence.summary: Modern pharmacology supports the topical wound-healing direction (allantoin, mucilage, RCT evidence) but EMA and toxicological reviews prohibit internal use owing to hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Culpeper chiefly recommends the root decoction for internal indications — inward ulcers, bloody flux, spitting of blood — which modern safety evidence directly contradicts.

concordance.rationale: Culpeper's principal recommendation is internal use of the root decoction for inward ulcers, bloody flux and spitting of blood. Modern evidence confirms topical wound-healing activity, but EMA restricts comfrey to unbroken skin and toxicological literature documents hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids. The historical internal indications are therefore contradicted by modern safety evidence.
concordance.uncertainty: Historical text is unambiguous about internal use and toxicological evidence is strong. Residual uncertainty concerns whether 17th-century root preparations carried materially lower PA loads than modern material.
caveats: Historical 'inward' indications were interpreted as internal use rather than topical poulticing.
EMA restriction applies to unbroken skin and limited duration of topical use.
Pyrrolizidine alkaloid content varies by species, plant part and harvest.

source_text:
AGRIMONY.

Descript :] Common Agrimony riseth up with round brownish stalks, two or three feet high, set with fine dented leaves, and at the tops small yellow flowers one above another, like unto a long spike.

Names :] It is called also Egrimoyne, Church Steeples, and Sticklewort; it grows in hedges and borders of fields.

Government and virtues :] It is under Jupiter and the sign of Cancer. The decoction of the herb, made with wine, and drunk, is good against the biting of serpents, and helps them that make bloody water. It healeth all inward ulcers, and outward sores and wounds, and stayeth bleedings. The leaves boiled in wine, and given to drink, help the colic. A syrup made of the juice and sugar is effectual for inward ulcers. Dioscorides saith, that it helpeth those that are bursten, that have bloody fluxes. The decoction gargled in the mouth easeth the pains of the toothache, and fasteneth loose teeth, and helpeth inflammations of the throat. It is a safe herb, and none need forbid the use of it.

resolutions.reasoning: Culpeper's description — 'small yellow flowers one above another, like unto a long spike' with 'fine dented leaves' — matches Agrimonia eupatoria, the agrimony of the English Pharmacopoeia; POWO returns the accepted name directly.

candidates.matched_via: vernacular 'fragrant agrimony' recorded in some counties

resolutions.reasoning: 'Church Steeples' was applied to agrimony generally and occasionally to A. procera (fragrant agrimony). The spike-flowered, non-fragrant description favours A. eupatoria but the vernacular alone is not decisive.
No authority source maps 'Sticklewort' to a modern taxon with confidence above threshold; recorded for both agrimony species in historical glossaries. Left unresolved.

ema_monograph.title: Agrimoniae herba — EMA/HMPC community monograph
ema_monograph.relevance_note: Traditional use for mild gastrointestinal complaints; topical use for minor inflammation of the skin. Does not cover serpent bites.

pubmed.title: Agrimonia eupatoria L.: phytochemistry, ethnomedicinal uses and pharmacological activities
pubmed.relevance_note: Review; supports anti-inflammatory and wound-healing directions.

pubmed.title: Anti-inflammatory activity of Agrimonia eupatoria extract in vitro and in vivo
pubmed.relevance_note: Mechanistic support for topical and mucosal claims only.

evidence.summary: Anti-inflammatory and astringent activity of Agrimonia eupatoria supports the topical wound and throat claims; internal organ claims (serpent bites, colic) rest on traditional-use plausibility and EMA traditional-use status only, with no clinical trials on the specific historical indications.

concordance.rationale: Topical wound-healing and mucosal anti-inflammatory activity of Agrimonia eupatoria is supported by phytochemical, in-vitro and EMA traditional-use evidence. Internal claims (serpent bites, colic, bloody flux) are plausible under astringent pharmacology but unproven; hence a moderate concordance grade.
concordance.uncertainty: No clinical trials address the specific historical indications; confidence derives from constituent pharmacology and regulatory traditional-use recognition.
caveats: EMA monograph covers gastrointestinal and topical indications, not serpent bites.
A. eupatoria is easily confused with A. procera in vernacular sources; part of the entry is resolved only ambiguously.
